name: Lock-Free Atomics
tagline: Coordinating shared state via hardware Compare-And-Swap (CAS) and memory orderings so at least one thread always makes progress.
purpose: Understand hardware CAS primitives, progress guarantees (lock-free vs wait-free), memory orderings, and how to prevent the ABA problem and false sharing.

spark.summary: Lock-free atomics coordinate shared state across threads using hardware compare-and-swap (CAS) primitives and explicit memory orderings so at least one thread always makes progress without OS mutex blocking.
spark.keyTakeaway: Lock-free atomics eliminate mutex context switches and deadlocks, but high contention still causes CPU cache-line bouncing—and pointer-based structures require ABA protection and safe memory reclamation.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** **Lock-free atomics** coordinate threads using hardware instructions—`CMPXCHG` on x86-64 or Load-Linked/Store-Conditional (`LDXR`/`STXR`) on ARM64—backed by the CPU's **MESI/MOESI cache coherence** protocol.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Compare-And-Swap (CAS) Optimistic Retry State Machine (1. LOAD -> 2. CMPXCHG -> 3. COMMITTED); How the ABA Problem Corrupts a Naive CAS Stack (Thread 1 -> Atomic Head -> Thread 2).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Match synchronization primitives to contention level and invariant complexity. Production lock-free runtimes (such as Rust `crossbeam-epoch` or Disruptor) combine **64-byte cache-line padding** (eliminating false sharing between producer/consumer cursors).

**Failure Modes & Application:** Explore memory barriers, false sharing, and thread-safe queue implementations.

learningJourney.title: What are Lock-Free Atomics
learningJourney.explanation:
**Lock-free atomics** coordinate threads using hardware instructions—`CMPXCHG` on x86-64 or Load-Linked/Store-Conditional (`LDXR`/`STXR`) on ARM64—backed by the CPU's **MESI/MOESI cache coherence** protocol.

Progress guarantees form a strict hierarchy: **wait-free** (every thread finishes in bounded steps), **lock-free** (system-wide, at least one thread finishes in finite steps even if others stall), and **obstruction-free** (progress only in isolation).

learningJourney.title: Why mutexes stall—and the ABA & Use-After-Free traps
learningJourney.explanation:
Under heavy multi-core contention, OS mutexes trigger scheduler preemption, priority inversion, and lock convoys. Uncontended CAS takes 5–15 ns with zero kernel syscalls.

However, lock-free pointer structures introduce two subtle hazards:
- **The ABA Problem**: Thread 1 reads `head = A`, pauses; Thread 2 pops `A`, pops `B`, and pushes `A` back. Thread 1's `CAS(&head, A, B)` succeeds even though `B` was freed!
- **Use-After-Free**: freeing a popped node while a concurrent reader still dereferences its `next` pointer.

benefits: 5–15 ns uncontended; zero deadlocks or priority inversion.
costs: Spins CPU under heavy single-word write contention; needs EBR/Hazard Pointers for nodes.

benefits: Distributes updates across per-core cache-padded cells to eliminate MESI bouncing.

learningJourney.title: Epoch-Based Reclamation & Cache-Line Isolation
learningJourney.explanation: Production lock-free runtimes (such as Rust `crossbeam-epoch` or Disruptor) combine **64-byte cache-line padding** (eliminating false sharing between producer/consumer cursors) with **Epoch-Based Reclamation (EBR)** so retired nodes are only freed once every active thread has advanced past the retirement epoch.

ideas.title: Avoid Overusing seq_cst
ideas.description: Use `relaxed` for standalone counters, `acquire`/`release` for producer-consumer handoffs, and reserve `seq_cst` only when total global ordering across multiple atomics is required.

ideas.description: Pack a 64-bit monotonic version counter alongside the 64-bit pointer to defeat ABA in lock-free stacks and freelists.

knowledgeCheck.question: How does Epoch-Based Reclamation (EBR) or Hazard Pointers solve safe memory reclamation in a lock-free linked list?

options.text: By wrapping every node pop in a global mutex
options.feedback: A global mutex breaks the lock-free progress guarantee.

options.text: By deferring physical memory freeing until no concurrent reader thread can still hold a reference to the unlinked node
options.feedback: Correct: EBR and Hazard Pointers track active reader epochs/pointers so retired nodes are freed only after all readers have moved past them.

options.text: By using std::memory_order_relaxed on all loads
options.feedback: Relaxed ordering does not prevent another thread from freeing memory while a reader dereferences it.

beginner.byteSummary:
**The Core Idea (Beginner):** **Lock-free atomics** coordinate threads using hardware instructions—`CMPXCHG` on x86-64 or Load-Linked/Store-Conditional (`LDXR`/`STXR`) on ARM64—backed by the CPU's **MESI/MOESI cache coherence** protocol.

**How It Flows:** Think of Lock-Free Atomics as a clear step-by-step chain: 1. LOAD -> 2. CMPXCHG -> 3. COMMITTED -> Thread 1 -> Atomic Head.

**Why Beginners Should Care:** Lock-free atomics eliminate mutex context switches and deadlocks, but high contention still causes CPU cache-line bouncing—and pointer-based structures require ABA protection and safe memory reclamation.
